554.title: Why do we hate?
554.hook: Sakka, king of the gods, asks why beings who wish to live without hate still live in hate
554.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the chain in Sakka's questions to show how conflict starts in the mind, and in Theravada countries Sakka is a familiar figure in temple art and stories as a devoted protector of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a jeweled city returned to thatch, and your line, all gone now. What fine thing did you enjoy, knowing it would pass? Today, a king of the gods arrives with a musician and a question. Day five hundred fifty-four.

Before the question, a love song. Sakka, king of the gods, wants to see the Buddha, who is sitting in a cave in the hills near Rajagaha. He doesn't just walk in. He sends ahead a celestial musician, Pancasikha, with a lute. Pancasikha stands near the cave and sings a song that mixes praise of the Buddha with longing for a girl he loves. The Buddha listens, and then tells him, kindly: the strings and your voice blend well. Then Sakka comes in, and asks something every newspaper still asks. Today: why do we hate?
screen: `A LOVE SONG OUTSIDE A CAVE.` → `THE STRINGS AND VOICE BLEND WELL.` → `THE KING OF THE GODS ASKS.`

segments.voice: The Sakkapanha, Sakka's questions, is the twenty-first Long Discourse. The first question goes like this. Gods, humans, and every other kind of being all wish to live without hate, without violence, without enemies, without ill will. And yet they live in hate, with violence, with enemies. Why? Notice the shape. Not, why are other people hateful? Everyone wants peace. Everyone ends up in conflict anyway. What's tying them? The Buddha answers: envy and stinginess. Envy, at what someone else has. Stinginess, about what you have. Sakka is pleased, and asks the obvious next question: and where do those come from? From what we hold dear and what we don't. And that? From desire, wanting. And desire? From thinking, the mind turning something over. And thinking? From what the sutta calls the spreading of perception: the mind taking one small thing and running with it, building a story, then another story on top. Each answer goes one layer down, like peeling a root. And it ends somewhere surprisingly ordinary. Hate between nations, and between neighbors, starts in the same place: a mind that proliferates. So the Buddha's answer is both bleak and hopeful. Bleak, because the root is in everyone. Hopeful, because it's in a place you can watch. Sakka says, as each answer lands: so it is, Blessed One. My doubt is cut off.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS PEACE. WHY NOT?` · `ENVY AND STINGINESS.` · `DEAR, DESIRE, THINKING.` · `THE MIND THAT SPREADS.` · then, large: `WHY DO WE HATE?`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask one honest question about yourself. Not about anyone else. Something like: who do I resent right now, and what do I want that they have? Or: what am I holding tightly? Don't answer quickly. Ask it, then breathe, and see if the answer goes one layer deeper on its own, the way Sakka's questions did. If the mind starts building a story, notice the building. The bell holds the time.
Why do we hate? Sakka's first question in DN 21; the Buddha answers envy and stinginess, rooted in what we hold dear, desire, and the spreading mind. Today's word.
Your line: why do we hate. Today, when resentment flares, ask one layer down: what am I envious of, or holding onto? Day five hundred fifty-four.

he asks why all beings, who wish to live without hate, still live in it.

then he traces them back, layer by layer.
the Buddha scolds Pancasikha for singing a love song

options: how to punish the envious.

whether the gods are free of them.
fork.reveal: he asks for the source, again and again, until the answer reaches the spreading of perception in the mind.

original.note: Pali issa-macchariya: envy and stinginess, the fetters the Buddha names for Sakka.

trapdoor: what you thought: hatred comes from bad people.
what it means: the Buddha traces it back to envy and stinginess, then to desire and thinking, in everyone.
what a scholar hears: DN 21 traces issa-macchariya back through piyappiya, chanda and vitakka to papanca-sanna-sankha, one of the canon's key passages on papanca.

555.title: The great foundations
555.hook: the long satipatthana, with the four truths expanded
555.howItsDone: In Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Thailand the Mahasatipatthana Sutta is often chanted in full, sometimes at the bedside of the dying, and many modern meditation methods trace themselves to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sakka's question, and your line, why do we hate. Did you find a layer underneath a resentment? Today, the discourse many teachers call the heart of meditation, in its longest form. Day five hundred fifty-five.

Some recipes come in two versions. The card in the drawer: flour, butter, sugar, bake. And the version your aunt dictates over the phone for forty minutes, with every step explained and every way it can go wrong. The teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness also comes in two versions in the Pali canon. One sits in the Middle-Length Discourses, and we met it there. The other is here, the twenty-second Long Discourse, and it's longer for one reason. Today: the great foundations.
screen: `THE CARD AND THE PHONE CALL.` → `TWO VERSIONS IN THE CANON.` → `ONE IS LONGER. WHY?`

segments.voice: It's the Mahasatipatthana Sutta, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. It opens among the Kurus with a bold line: this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for overcoming sorrow and lament, for the ending of pain and grief, for realizing nibbana. Namely, the four foundations. Then the four, as before. Body: the breath, the postures, clear awareness in every action, the parts of the body, the elements, the charnel ground. Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. Mind: with greed or without, with hate or without. And mental qualities: the hindrances, the heaps, the senses, the factors of awakening, and the four noble truths. And here the long version slows right down. What is the truth of suffering? Birth, aging, death, sorrow, lament, pain, grief, despair, and each word is defined. Where does craving arise? Wherever something in the world seems pleasant and agreeable: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind, and then sights, sounds, smells, contacts, feelings, thoughts, one by one. Where does it cease? In exactly the same places. That repetition is the point. The long way doesn't add new ideas. It walks the same ground slowly enough that you can see craving start and stop in the most ordinary places. And at the end, a promise that shrinks. Whoever practices these four for seven years can expect a fruit. Never mind seven years: six, five, four, all the way down. Never mind a year: seven months, down to half a month. Never mind that: seven days.
screen: `THE DIRECT PATH, AMONG THE KURUS.` · `BODY, FEELING, MIND, QUALITIES.` · `THE FOUR TRUTHS, SLOWED RIGHT DOWN.` · `SEVEN YEARS, DOWN TO SEVEN DAYS.` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY.`

segments.voice: Walk the four foundations once, slowly. First, the body: feel where you're sitting and the breath moving. Then feeling: is this moment pleasant, unpleasant, or neither? Then mind: is it calm or restless, wanting or not? Then one mental quality: is a hindrance here, or something like interest, or ease? Then back to the body, and around again. After the bell, if you have time, keep going, up to fifteen minutes. The bell holds the time.
The great foundations. The Mahasatipatthana Sutta: the four foundations of mindfulness, with the four noble truths unfolded step by step. Today's word.
Your line: the long way. Today, pick one moment of wanting something, and walk it slowly: where did it start, what was pleasant, and where did it stop? Day five hundred fifty-five.

original.note: Pali satipatthana: sati, mindfulness; patthana or upatthana, foundation or establishing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the long and short versions of the sutta teach different things.
what it means: they teach the same four foundations; the long one walks through the four truths in detail.
what a scholar hears: DN 22 is MN 10 plus an expanded saccapabba; whether satipatthana means 'foundation' (patthana) or 'establishing' (upatthana) of mindfulness is debated.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta), the shorter parallel

556.title: The sceptic's parables
556.hook: Prince Payasi argues against rebirth; Kumara Kassapa answers with stories
556.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often retell the parables of the Payasi Sutta, especially the hemp carrier, when talking about holding views, and many traditions treat honest doubt as a question to explore rather than a fault.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the great foundations, and your line, the long way. Where did you watch a craving start and stop? Today, a long argument, and nobody in it is a villain. Day five hundred fifty-six.

Payasi is a ruler of the town of Setavya, and he has a firm view. There is no world after this one. No beings reborn. No fruit of good or bad deeds. And he's not lazy about it. He's tested it. He's asked dying friends who lived badly to come back and warn him, if there's anything after. None came. He's asked dying friends who lived well to come back and tell him. None came. So he concludes: nothing. When a monk named Kumara Kassapa comes through, Payasi goes out to argue. Today: the sceptic's parables.
screen: `NO WORLD BEYOND, SAYS PAYASI.` → `HE ASKED THE DYING TO RETURN.` → `NONE CAME.`

segments.voice: The Payasi Sutta, the twenty-third Long Discourse, is set after the Buddha's death, and it's almost all stories. To the first experiment, Kassapa answers with a thief. A man is caught, and on the way to execution he says: let me go home first, just to say goodbye. Would the guards let him? No. Then why expect someone in a hard rebirth to be allowed back to report? To the second, a man who has fallen into a pit of filth. He's pulled out, scrubbed, perfumed, dressed in fine clothes. Would he want to go back down into the pit? No. Then why expect someone in a happy world to come back here? Payasi tries harder experiments, and Kassapa answers with more stories. A village hears a conch for the first time and asks the shell to speak again, but it only sounds when someone blows it with effort. And at last, when Payasi admits he's half persuaded, but says he can't give up a view he's famous for, Kassapa tells the best one. Two friends find a bundle of hemp. Later they find hemp thread, then cloth, then silver, then gold. One friend swaps up each time. The other says: no, I've carried this hemp a long way, and it's well tied. And he walks home with the hemp. Notice how Kassapa argues. He never mocks. He treats Payasi's doubt as a real question that deserves a real answer, and answers it with pictures anyone can weigh. Whether you find the answers convincing is yours to decide. The sutta's respect for the question is plain.
screen: `A THIEF ON THE WAY TO EXECUTION.` · `A MAN PULLED FROM THE PIT.` · `THE SHELL THAT WON'T SPEAK ALONE.` · `THE MAN WHO KEPT HIS HEMP.` · then, large: `THE SCEPTIC'S PARABLES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one doubt you hold. About a teaching, about yourself, about anything. Don't try to settle it. Treat it the way Kassapa treated Payasi: as a fair question from someone worth talking to. Breathe with it. Then check, gently: am I keeping this view because I've weighed it, or because I've carried it a long way? Either answer is fine. Just notice. The bell holds the time.
The sceptic's parables. In DN 23 Kumara Kassapa answers Payasi's doubts about rebirth with stories, never with scorn. Today's word.
Your line: the sceptic's parables. Today, when someone doubts something you care about, answer their question respectfully, with a picture rather than a put-down. Day five hundred fifty-six.

what it means: Payasi tests his view seriously, and Kassapa answers him patiently with stories.
what a scholar hears: DN 23 is one of the canon's longest debates, built almost entirely of upamas, and sets an early Indian materialist position against rebirth and kamma.

557.title: Your own pasture
557.hook: be islands to yourselves; keep to your own ancestral pasture
557.howItsDone: Buddhist meditation teachers often describe the four foundations of mindfulness as the practitioner's home ground, and the hawk-and-quail story is a familiar teaching picture in many Theravada communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Payasi and Kassapa, and your line, the sceptic's parables. Did you answer a doubt with respect? Today we start a discourse that runs across three days, and it opens close to home. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

A quail is pecking in an open field when a hawk drops out of the sky and grabs it. As it's carried off, the quail laments: if only I'd stayed in my own ground, among the clods of the plowed field where my family has always lived, this hawk couldn't have touched me. The hawk, amused, lets it go: go on then, back to your ground, see if it saves you. The quail darts into the clods, and calls out a dare. The hawk dives, and the quail slips behind a clod. The hawk hits the earth. Today: your own pasture.
screen: `A QUAIL IN THE OPEN.` → `IF ONLY I'D STAYED HOME.` → `THE HAWK HITS THE CLOD.`

segments.voice: That quail story comes from the Connected Discourses. It's the best commentary on how the twenty-sixth Long Discourse opens, the Cakkavatti Sihanada, the lion's roar on the wheel-turning king. The Buddha is at Matula in Magadha, and he begins: monks, live as islands to yourselves, as your own refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as your island, the Dhamma as your refuge. Then the image the hawk and quail make vivid: keep to your own pasture, the range of your fathers. Walking there, Mara, the tempter, will get no chance at you. The Pali for pasture is gocara, literally where the cow walks, the ground an animal knows and feeds on. And what is a monk's own pasture? The Buddha says it plainly: the four foundations of mindfulness. Body, feeling, mind, and mental qualities. That's home ground. Notice what this doesn't mean. It doesn't mean stay in your bubble, or never go out. The quail isn't safe because it hides. It's safe because it's somewhere it knows well, where it has cover. Out in the open, in somebody else's territory, scrolling and comparing and chasing, the hawk can dive. Back on familiar ground, with attention resting on the breath, the body, what's actually happening, the hawk can't get a grip. And the discourse goes on from here into a long story about kings, wheels and the whole human future, which we'll follow over the next two days. But it starts with a bird finding its way home.
screen: `THE QUAIL AND THE HAWK.` · `ISLANDS TO YOURSELVES.` · `GOCARA: WHERE THE COW WALKS.` · `HOME GROUND: THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PASTURE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and come back to your own ground. Feel the body sitting: that's one clod in the field. Feel the breath: another. Notice whether this moment is pleasant or not: another. When the mind wanders out into the open, into plans or worries or other people's lives, notice the hawk's shadow, and step back behind the clod. No drama. Just home again. The bell holds the time.
Your own pasture. In DN 26 the Buddha says: keep to your own ground, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the tempter gets no chance. Today's word.
Your line: your own pasture. Today, when you feel yourself drifting into a field that isn't yours, come back to one breath, one footstep, and stay on your own ground. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: Poverty breeds violence
558.hook: a king neglects the poor; theft, then weapons, then killing follow
558.howItsDone: Buddhist social thinkers in Asia and beyond often cite the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta when they speak about poverty and crime, and many Buddhist communities run food banks, clinics and relief work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quail and the hawk, and your line, your own pasture. Did you come back to your own ground? Today the same discourse leaves the field and walks into a palace. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

In the old story there are wheel-turning kings, rulers so just that a great jeweled wheel appears in the sky and rolls ahead of them, and other kingdoms simply welcome them. The first, Dalhanemi, grows old, hands the throne to his son, and goes forth. The wheel vanishes. The son asks his father what to do, and is told: the wheel isn't an inheritance. You have to earn it. Rule by the Dhamma. Protect everyone, even the birds and beasts. And give wealth to those who have none. Generations later, a king forgets that last part. Today: poverty breeds violence.
screen: `A WHEEL IN THE SKY.` → `NOT AN INHERITANCE.` → `ONE KING FORGETS.`

segments.voice: This king, in the Cakkavatti Sihanada, rules by his own ideas. He protects people, but he doesn't give wealth to the needy. And so, the text says, poverty spreads. Then a man steals. He's caught and brought before the king. Why did you steal? Because I had nothing to live on, sire. So the king gives him money: live on this, support your parents, your wife and children, start a business, give to holy people. Good. But word gets around, and others steal, hoping for the same. Now the king panics. If I keep giving money to thieves, theft will only grow. So he does the opposite: he has the next thief bound, paraded through the streets to the beat of a harsh drum, and beheaded. And what happens? People hear, and think: then we'll carry sharp swords, and kill those we rob so nobody can report us. Theft becomes killing. Then lying, to cover it. Then slander, and on down a long list, and with every step, human life gets shorter and uglier. Look at the chain the sutta draws. The trouble doesn't start with a wicked thief. It starts with a king who didn't share. Then a harsh answer to a symptom makes it worse. It's an old Indian story, and the Buddha tells it as a story, with fantastic numbers and ages. But the chain it draws doesn't need the fantastic numbers: when people have nothing, and the only answer is punishment, the text says violence grows.
screen: `HE DIDN'T GIVE TO THE NEEDY.` · `THE FIRST THIEF IS HELPED.` · `THE NEXT ONE IS BEHEADED.` · `THEN EVERYONE CARRIES A SWORD.` · then, large: `POVERTY BREEDS VIOLENCE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who doesn't have enough. A person you pass on the street, a family you've heard about, a cause you care about. Let their situation be real for a moment, not an idea. Breathe with it. Then let one small, concrete thing come to mind that you could give: money, food, time, a phone call. You don't have to decide yet. Just let it be clear. The bell holds the time.
Poverty breeds violence. In DN 26 a king stops giving to the needy; theft follows, then a harsh punishment, then weapons and killing. Today's word.
Your line: poverty breeds violence. Today, give something real to someone in need, however small, the way the old kings were told to. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: People turn again
559.hook: human life shrinks, then people turn back to goodness; Metteyya will come
559.howItsDone: Buddhists across Asia honor Metteyya, or Maitreya, as the coming Buddha, often depicted seated with feet on the ground, ready to rise, and many make merit in the hope of meeting his teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a king who stopped sharing, and your line, poverty breeds violence. What did you give? Today the same story hits bottom, and then something turns. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

The Cakkavatti Sihanada keeps going down. With every new kind of wrongdoing, the story says, human lifespans shrink, from tens of thousands of years down and down, until people live just ten years. Fine foods disappear. The very idea of a good deed disappears; there's not even a word for good. People treat each other like animals. And then comes something the text calls a sword-interval: seven days in which people see each other as prey, and kill. It's as dark as anything in the canon. And it isn't the end. Today: people turn again.
screen: `LIFE SHRINKS TO TEN YEARS.` → `NO WORD FOR GOOD.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF SWORDS.`

segments.voice: During those seven days, some people slip away. They hide in long grass, in thickets, in forests, among rocks and rivers, living on roots and fruit. When the seven days are over, they come out. And they see each other, and they embrace. The story gives their words simply: how good to see living beings still alive! Then they talk. We lost so much because we took up wrong ways. What if we gave up just one thing? What if we stopped killing? And they do. Just that one. And their children live a little longer. Seeing this, they give up something else: taking what isn't given. Then lying. Then harsh speech. Step by step, each generation adds one good thing, and human life lengthens again, all the way back to eighty thousand years. Then, the Buddha says, a Buddha named Metteyya will arise in the world, as I have arisen now, and he will teach the same Dhamma, good in the beginning, the middle and the end, and lead a community of many thousands, as I lead hundreds. Two things stand out. First, the turn starts with one small change, made by frightened people who are simply glad to see each other alive. Not a hero, not a king. Second, the hope is long. Many Buddhists in many lands look forward to Metteyya, known in Sanskrit as Maitreya, the Buddha to come. Metteyya's name is often linked with metta, loving-kindness. After all that darkness, the future has a kind name.
screen: `THE ONES WHO HID.` · `HOW GOOD TO SEE YOU ALIVE.` · `ONE GOOD THING AT A TIME.` · `METTEYYA WILL COME.` · then, large: `PEOPLE TURN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the picture of the survivors come: people stepping out of the forest, seeing each other, glad. Breathe with that gladness. Then look forward, not with worry but with hope. Picture one good change that could spread, one generation adding one thing. Maybe it's something you could start. Rest with that future for a while. The bell holds the time.
People turn again. In DN 26, after the worst, survivors give up killing, then one wrong after another, and life grows long until Metteyya comes. Today's word.
Your line: people turn again. Today, when the news is bleak, look for one small good change someone is making, and be glad of it. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

560.title: They tasted the earth
560.hook: beings of light taste the earth's savory crust and grow coarse
560.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell the Agganna Sutta as a story about craving and pride rather than a scientific account, and mindful eating, with attention to each bite, is practiced in many Buddhist monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: survivors coming out of the forest, and your line, people turn again. What good change did you notice? Today closes a week, with a very old story about the first bite. Day five hundred sixty.

Two young men, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, were born brahmins and are training to become monks. Their families are furious. Brahmins, they're told, are the highest class, born from Brahma's own mouth. The Buddha smiles at that: brahmin women are seen pregnant and giving birth, just like everyone else. Born from Brahma's mouth? Then he tells them how things really started, at least in the story he tells. It's the twenty-seventh Long Discourse, the Agganna, the discourse on beginnings. Today: they tasted the earth.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS BECOMING MONKS.` → `BORN FROM BRAHMA'S MOUTH?` → `A STORY OF BEGINNINGS.`

segments.voice: There comes a time, the story goes, when the world rolls up and comes apart, and beings are reborn in a realm of radiance. They are made of mind, feed on joy, shine with their own light, and move through the air. Then the world rolls out again, all water and darkness, no sun, no moon. And over the water spreads a savory earth, like the skin that forms on hot milk as it cools. It has the color of fine ghee and tastes like pure honey. Then one being, the text says, of a greedy nature, wonders: what can this be? and tastes it with a finger. It's delicious. Craving comes. Others copy him. Soon they're breaking off lumps with their hands. And as they eat, their own light fades. Then the sun and moon appear, and night and day, and seasons. Their bodies grow coarse. Some look better than others, and the better-looking ones grow proud. And with that pride, the savory earth vanishes. They gather and lament: oh, the taste! The story then goes on, step by step, through coarser foods. Look at what drives it. Not a curse, not a punishment from above. Just tasting, wanting more, comparing, pride. Many scholars hear gentle humor here too, a story built to answer the brahmins' claims. Look back at the week: why do we hate, the great foundations, the sceptic's parables, your own pasture, poverty breeds violence, people turn again, and now beings of light, licking a finger.

segments.voice: If you have something small to eat nearby, a raisin, a piece of bread, a sip of tea, take it now. Before you taste, look at it. Smell it. Then take the smallest bite, and let it sit on the tongue. Notice the first flavor, and then notice the wanting that comes right after: more. Don't fight it. Just see it arrive, like the first being with the finger. If there's nothing to eat, do this with a breath. The bell holds the time.
They tasted the earth. In DN 27 shining beings taste the savory crust of the new world; craving and pride follow, and their light fades. Today's word.
